entities.name: Herihor
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Herihor, a formidable figure in the late 11th century BCE (fl. c. 1080–1074 BCE), stands as a pivotal architect in the fragmentation of Egypt's centralized authority, marking the transition from the unified New Kingdom to the fractured Third Intermediate Period. Rising from a military commander and vizier under the 20th Dynasty pharaoh Ramesses XI, Herihor ultimately seized de facto control of Upper Egypt, consolidating immense power as the High Priest of Amun at Thebes. His ascent, concurrent with the profound decline of the pharaonic institution, created a dual monarchy, with Herihor and his successors ruling the south from Thebes, while weak pharaohs nominally controlled the Delta, irrevocably altering the geopolitical landscape of ancient Egypt.

His career trajectory saw him accumulate an array of powerful titles: 'Overseer of the Granaries,' 'Commander of the Army,' and 'Vizier,' before his decisive move to claim the supreme religious office of High Priest of Amun at Karnak. This position granted him control over the immense wealth and landholdings of the Amun priesthood, effectively making him the wealthiest and most influential man in Upper Egypt. By approximately 1080 BCE, Herihor had begun to adopt royal prerogatives, including inscribing his name in cartouches and commissioning building projects, effectively operating as an independent monarch. He initiated the restoration of royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings, a testament to his assumption of traditional pharaonic duties, and his authority extended over Nubia, maintaining Egypt's southern frontier during a period of internal upheaval.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Herihor's actions irrevocably divided Egypt into two spheres of influence, initiating the Third Intermediate Period and establishing a powerful, long-lasting priestly dynasty in Upper Egypt that lasted for nearly four centuries.
